fields.title: C. S. Lewis (For Teens)
fields.description: At nine, Jack Lewis prayed for his dying mother to get well, and then for her to come back to life. Nothing happened, and by fourteen he had decided there was no God. He survived a shell in the trenches, kept a dead friend's promise for more than thirty years, and was hunted down, as he saw it, by the God he had denied, before he wrote Narnia and married a dying woman at her hospital bedside. This teen edition tells his life straight: the lies, the doubts, the grief, and the slow change God worked in him.

qa.question: Who was C. S. Lewis?
qa.answer: A writer and scholar from Belfast, born in 1898, who lost his faith as a boy, fought and was wounded in the First World War, and came back to God in his early thirties. He taught at Oxford and Cambridge, gave wartime radio talks that became Mere Christianity, wrote The Screwtape Letters and the Narnia books, and died in 1963.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It tells how he lied to his father for years, admits that nobody knows the full truth about his relationship with Mrs Moore, and covers his pride, his brother's drinking, his wife's cancer and the grief that made him wonder whether God was cruel.

qa.question: What did Lewis mean by calling himself “the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England”?
qa.answer: He was describing the night he knelt and admitted that God was God. He had resisted for years and gave in without joy, because he could no longer find anywhere to hide. At that point he believed in God but not yet in Christ.

qa.question: Did losing a debate to Elizabeth Anscombe make him give up defending Christianity?
qa.answer: No. In 1948 she showed that one of his arguments was flawed, and he took it seriously and rewrote the chapter. But he went on leading the Socratic Club and writing Christian books for the rest of his life, and Anscombe herself called the legend nonsense.

qa.question: How did he treat other people?
qa.answer: He cared for Mrs Moore for more than thirty years, gave two-thirds of his royalties away through a charity, answered thousands of letters from strangers by hand, and supported Joy's son David when he chose to live as an observant Jew. He could also be overbearing in argument, and he knew it.

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length biography of C. S. Lewis, which draws on his own account of his early life, his letters, his brother's diaries and the work of his biographers, and says plainly where the sources disagree, such as the year he came to believe in God.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from his story?
qa.answer: That God can pursue you even while you run; that honest doubt and grief are not the end of faith; that keeping your word matters; and that real change in a person usually comes slowly, through ordinary habits like prayer, honesty and serving the people around you.

qa.question: Was his marriage to Joy Davidman like the film Shadowlands?
qa.answer: Not exactly. The film changed the ages of Joy's sons, left one of them out and invented scenes. In fact they married first at a register office so she could stay in England, then again at her hospital bedside in 1957 when she was thought to be dying, and had about three more years together.

fields.title: Call Me Jack
fields.body_html:
“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.” — Proverbs 22:6 (KJV)

Clive Staples Lewis was born on 29 November 1898 in Belfast, a city of shipyards, linen mills and rope works in the north of Ireland. From the hills near his home you could see the giant cranes of the Harland and Wolff yard, where the Titanic would soon be built.

While he was still very small, he announced that he would no longer answer to Clive. He had decided to be named after a neighbourhood dog called Jacksie, and he held out until his family gave in. Jacksie became Jacks, and Jacks became Jack. To the people who loved him he was Jack for the rest of his life. Only the outside world called him Clive, and later C. S. Lewis.

His father, Albert, was a solicitor who worked in the police courts. He was clever and emotional, fond of long words and big speeches, and an anxious man who loved his sons deeply but never found an easy way to show it. His mother, Flora, was quiet, funny and remarkably well educated. She had taken an honours degree in logic and mathematics at a time when very few women anywhere went to university, and she taught Jack the beginnings of French and Latin herself.

His best friend was his brother. Warren, whom everyone called Warnie, was three and a half years older. One day Warnie brought into the nursery the lid of a biscuit tin covered with moss, twigs and flowers: a tiny toy garden. Jack remembered it as the first beautiful thing he ever saw, and it stirred in him a sudden, aching longing he could not explain. That longing came back again and again as he grew up, at the sight of far-off hills, in a story, in a line of poetry. Much later he came to believe it was one of the threads by which God had been drawing him.

Jack was short-sighted, clumsy with his hands because of a defect in his thumb joints, and hopeless at games. So he drew and wrote. He and Warnie invented a whole imaginary world called Boxen, with its own history, maps, politics and even railway timetables. The stories, which still survive, are full of parliaments and cabinet plots.

In 1905, when Jack was six, the family moved into a big new house called Little Lea. It was rambling and draughty, full of long corridors, empty rooms and attics, and above all full of books. They were in almost every room and stacked in the attics, and nobody stopped him reading any of them. On long rainy afternoons he read the old poets and novelists years before any school set them.

The family went to church at St Mark's, where Jack's grandfather was the rector. Jack learned his prayers and said them. Nobody forced faith on him, but there is no sign that it went deep either. He took Christianity for granted, the way he took Little Lea for granted, without asking what it rested on.

One more thing is worth knowing now. Years later Jack wrote about his father in a way that made Albert look a bit ridiculous, and many readers think that was unfair. Albert worked hard to give his sons an education he had never had, and he went on supporting Jack long after most fathers would have stopped. In his later years Lewis deeply regretted how he had treated his father. That regret will come back in this story.

The verse at the top of this chapter is a promise to parents: train a child in the right way, and when he is old he will not leave it. For a long time it looked as if that promise had failed for Jack. But Proverbs is talking about the end of the story, not the middle. If you have grown up around faith and you are not sure yet what it means to you, you are not the first. God is patient with the middle.

One thing to do this week: make a list of three things that have given you that same kind of longing: a place, a song, a story, a view. Next to each one, write one sentence about what you think you were really longing for.

study_questions.answer: As a small boy he refused to answer to Clive and insisted on being named after a neighbourhood dog called Jacksie. The name shortened to Jacks and then Jack, and his family and friends used it for the rest of his life.

study_questions.question: What did Warnie's toy garden stir in Jack?
study_questions.answer: A sudden, aching longing he couldn't explain. It came back throughout his childhood, and later he believed it was one of the ways God had been drawing him.

study_questions.question: How did Lewis later feel about the way he had treated his father?
study_questions.answer: He deeply regretted it. Many readers think his written picture of Albert was unfair, and friends said it weighed on him more than almost anything in his past.

fields.title: August 1908
fields.body_html:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.” — Psalm 27:10 (KJV)

Early in 1908 Flora Lewis was found to have cancer. In those days operations were often done at home, and hers was carried out at Little Lea while the household tried to carry on around it. For a while she seemed to get better. Then, in the summer, the disease came back. The house filled with nurses, doctors and the smell of antiseptic. Jack and Warnie were kept out of the sickroom, and nobody explained much. They only knew that everything had changed.

It was a terrible year for their father too. Albert's own father died that spring, his wife was dying through the summer, and within weeks of her death his brother died as well. Under that weight Albert became almost a stranger to his sons: given to outbursts of grief and temper, lost in his own suffering, unable to reach the two frightened boys who were watching him.

Jack prayed. He had been taught that God answers prayer, and he believed it the way a nine-year-old believes things. He prayed that his mother would get well. She died on 23 August 1908, aged forty-six. Then he prayed that she would come back to life. Nothing happened.

Nearly fifty years later, Lewis was careful about how he described this. He did not say it was the moment he lost his faith. He thought he had been treating God less like a Saviour and more like a magician who would do the trick and then go away. When the trick didn't work, he wasn't shattered; he was simply left with nothing. But he believed it laid the foundation for the unbelief that came later.

On the day Flora died, the page on the Shakespeare calendar in her bedroom carried a line from King Lear: “Men must endure their going hence.” Albert kept the page. Remember that line. It comes back at the very end of this book.

Jack remembered being taken in to see his mother's body and being horrified: it was not the face he knew. He hated the flowers, the hearse and the black clothes. After that, he and Warnie drew closer together and further from their father. They loved Albert and pitied him, but they stopped trusting him with their real lives. It was the start of a habit of hiding that would last twenty years.

Less than a month after the funeral, Albert sent both boys to boarding school in England. They crossed the Irish Sea on the night boat, and Jack never forgot the misery of it: the smell, the dark, the grey dawn, the feeling of being carried away from everything he knew. The school, Wynyard, was a bad one. Its headmaster beat the boys for little or no reason and taught them almost nothing, and he was later certified insane. Yet it was there, of all places, that Jack was taken to a church where the faith was taught as if it mattered, and for a short time he prayed seriously and read his Bible.

Psalm 27 doesn't promise that you will never feel abandoned. It says what God does when you are: “then the LORD will take me up.” Neither of Jack's parents meant to forsake him, but a child can feel forsaken anyway. If you have lost someone, or prayed hard for something that didn't happen, you are allowed to feel it. Lewis didn't see God's answer for many years. But it came, and later he wrote to grieving strangers with a tenderness that came straight from that wound.

One thing to do this week: if there is a prayer you feel God ignored, write it down. Don't tidy it up. Then talk about it with someone you trust. If grief feels too heavy to carry, tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher or a doctor.

fields.title: A Faith Let Go
fields.body_html:
“Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.” — Matthew 6:8 (KJV)

Wynyard closed in 1910 for lack of pupils. After one term at a school in Belfast, Jack was sent in 1911 to Cherbourg House, a much better school in the English spa town of Malvern. He worked hard there and in 1913 won a scholarship. But it was at Cherbourg, between the ages of twelve and fourteen, that he quietly stopped being a Christian. Looking back, he gave several reasons, and none of them was dramatic.

One was a kind school matron who had drifted from ordinary Christianity into a vague mix of spiritualism and theosophy, and who talked about it to the boys. She wasn't trying to unsettle anyone. But to a clever, lonely boy, her talk made the plain faith he had grown up with seem less solid.

A second reason was the way he had been trying to pray. At Wynyard he had decided that a prayer didn't count unless he felt the right things while saying it. So he would lie awake night after night, saying his prayers over and over, trying to produce the proper feelings and never succeeding. It became a torment. Later he thought this kind of religion, which put all the weight on his own feelings instead of on God, made faith a burden he was glad to drop. When he dropped it, the relief was enormous.

A third reason went deeper. He noticed the waste and cruelty of the world. He saw that modern scholars treated the old gods of Greece and Rome as fables, and he couldn't see why the Christian God should be treated any differently. Nobody gave him an answer that satisfied him, and he didn't much want one. So, without telling anyone, he stopped believing. He kept going to chapel because it was expected. Inside, he was done with it.

In 1913 he followed Warnie to Malvern College. Warnie had loved it. Jack hated it from the first week. The school was run by the senior boys, and the younger boys were their servants, cleaning shoes and running errands at all hours. Everything revolved around sport, which he was useless at, and around popularity and power. He also hated the school's moral life: the snobbery, the social climbing, and a culture of favouritism among the boys, some of it sexual, which he wrote about frankly forty years later. Warnie thought Jack's account was too bitter, and the truth probably lies somewhere between them. But Jack was miserable, and his lifelong distrust of the desire to belong to the inner ring, the in-crowd, started there.

There were bright spots: a good library, a teacher who loved poetry, and the old Norse myths, which he devoured. And in the Easter holidays of 1914, back in Belfast, he visited a boy across the road who was ill in bed. His name was Arthur Greeves. On the bed lay a book of Norse mythology. Arthur asked whether Jack liked it, and Jack said he did. In a moment, each discovered that the other loved exactly the same things. They wrote to each other for nearly fifty years, and Jack told Arthur things he told nobody else, including, one day, the story of how he came back to God.

Jesus told his followers not to pray like people who think they will be heard for their many words, because “your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.” Jack's problem wasn't that he prayed too little. It was that he made prayer about his own feelings instead of about God. Plenty of people do the same, and when the feelings don't come, they decide God isn't there. Feelings come and go. God doesn't depend on them.

One thing to do this week: pray once a day without checking how it feels. Say something honest and short, then stop. At the end of the week, notice whether it was harder or easier than you expected.

study_questions.question: Name two reasons Jack gave for losing his faith at Cherbourg.
study_questions.answer: Any two of these: a matron's vague spiritualism loosened his faith; his anxious attempts to make himself feel the right things in prayer made religion a torment; and he could not see why Christianity should be true when the old myths were treated as fables.

study_questions.answer: The rule of the senior boys, the worship of games, the snobbery and social climbing, and a culture of favouritism among the boys. It left him with a lifelong distrust of wanting to belong to the inner ring.

study_questions.question: How did Jack and Arthur Greeves become friends?
study_questions.answer: Jack visited Arthur when he was ill in bed, saw a book of Norse myths beside him, and found they loved exactly the same things. They wrote to each other for nearly fifty years.

fields.title: The Great Knock
fields.body_html:
“Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.” — Proverbs 27:17 (KJV)

Jack's letters home from Malvern were so wretched that even Albert could see something had to change. In September 1914, a month after the First World War broke out, fifteen-year-old Jack arrived in the village of Great Bookham, in Surrey, to be tutored for university by William Kirkpatrick, Albert's own old headmaster. The family called him the Great Knock. He was tall, lean and ruthless in argument, with side whiskers and a voice like a bell. He had been brought up a Presbyterian and had become a convinced atheist. He didn't talk about religion much. He simply assumed no intelligent person could believe it.

On the walk from the station, Jack tried some polite conversation: the Surrey countryside, he said, was wilder than he had expected. Kirkpatrick stopped him. What did he mean by wild? What grounds did he have for expecting anything else? Within minutes the boy had been shown that he had no clear idea what he meant, no evidence, and so no right to an opinion at all. Many boys would have been crushed. Jack loved it. For the first time in his life a grown man was taking him seriously.

He learned to define his words, look for evidence, spot a bad argument from a long way off, and say exactly what he meant. Kirkpatrick taught languages just as directly. On the first morning he opened Homer in Greek, read and translated a passage aloud, and left Jack to carry on with a dictionary. Soon Jack was reading Homer at speed. Before he left, he had added French, Italian and some German. Those two and a half years were among the happiest of his life, and the clear, sharp way he wrote for the rest of his life was learned in that house.

He also settled into his unbelief. By sixteen he was writing to Arthur, with all the confidence of youth, that every religion was a mythology invented by human beings, and that he believed in none of them.

Then came something he regretted for the rest of his life. In December 1914 he was confirmed at his home church in Belfast and took his first Communion. He didn't believe a word of it. He did it to please his father, and because he couldn't face the argument if he refused. Years later he counted it among the worst things he had ever done: a solemn act before God, made out of cowardice.

In March 1916, waiting for a train at Leatherhead station, he bought a cheap book from the bookstall: Phantastes, a fairy-tale romance by George MacDonald, a Scottish minister turned writer. He read it that night and was overwhelmed. He had no idea MacDonald was a Christian, and the book didn't argue him into anything. But he felt that a new kind of goodness had touched his old longing, as if it had been washed clean. He later said, in effect, that the book had begun to work on his imagination, and that the rest of him took much longer to follow. It took fifteen years. MacDonald became the writer Lewis loved above all others, and he called him his master.

Proverbs says iron sharpens iron. Here an old atheist sharpened a young one, and the edge he put on Jack's mind would one day be used to defend everything Kirkpatrick rejected. God can use people who don't believe in him to get you ready. A tough teacher, a hard question, a friend who disagrees with you: none of it has to be wasted.

And notice that confirmation. Pretending to believe to keep the peace is easy, and it's common. Lewis didn't shrug it off. Being honest with God matters more than looking right in front of people.

One thing to do this week: the next time someone challenges something you say, don't get defensive. Ask yourself Kirkpatrick's two questions: what exactly do I mean, and what are my reasons? Then write down one thing you believe and your honest reasons for it.

study_questions.question: What happened on Jack's first walk with Kirkpatrick?
study_questions.answer: Jack remarked that Surrey was wilder than he expected, and Kirkpatrick made him define “wild” and give his grounds, showing him he had no clear meaning or evidence. Jack loved being taken seriously.

study_questions.question: Why did Lewis later regret his confirmation in 1914?
study_questions.answer: He didn't believe any of it. He went through with it to please his father and avoid an argument, and he later saw it as a solemn act before God done out of cowardice.

study_questions.question: What did reading Phantastes do for Jack?
study_questions.answer: It didn't convince him of anything, but he felt a new kind of goodness touch his longing. It began to work on his imagination years before the rest of him came to faith.

On the walk from the station, Jack tried some polite conversation: the Surrey countryside, he said, was wilder than he had expected. Kirkpatrick stopped him. What did he mean by wild? Many boys would have been crushed. Jack loved it. For the first time in his life a grown man was taking him seriously. He learned to define his words, look for evidence, spot a bad argument from a long way off, and say exactly what he meant. Kirkpatrick taught languages just as directly. On the first morning he opened Homer in Greek, read and translated a passage aloud, and left Jack to carry on with a dictionary. Soon Jack was reading Homer at speed. “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.” — Ecclesiastes 5:4 (KJV)

In December 1916 Jack won a scholarship to University College, Oxford. There was one problem. To get in, everyone had to pass an exam that included basic maths, and Jack, who could translate Homer at sight, could not do sums. He failed it. In the end the war solved it for him: afterwards, men who had served were excused.

He arrived at Oxford in April 1917, but the war had emptied the place. As an Irishman he was exempt from conscription. He chose to serve anyway. In June he joined a cadet battalion housed in Keble College, two to a room. His roommate was Paddy Moore, almost exactly his age and also Irish. Paddy's mother, Janie Moore, had come to Oxford to be near her son, bringing his eleven-year-old sister Maureen. She was forty-five, warm, talkative and generous, separated from a husband she called the Beast, and in the habit of mothering every young man her son brought home. To an eighteen-year-old who had lost his mother at nine and lived among schoolmasters ever since, her kitchen table meant a great deal.

At some point in those months Jack and Paddy made a promise. If one of them was killed and the other survived, the survivor would look after the dead man's parent. We know about it from Maureen, who remembered it years later, and from the way Jack lived afterwards, which only makes sense if the promise was real. Many young officers made pacts like that. Few kept one the way Jack did.

He reached the front line in France on 29 November 1917, his nineteenth birthday. He said very little about the war afterwards: a few lines about the cold, the mud, the wounded and the unburied dead. He never pretended to have been a brave soldier. He did his duty, endured, and later tried, with only partial success, to forget.

The sergeant next to him, Harry Ayres, a kind, steady man who had looked after his young officer, was killed outright. A fragment of metal stayed in Jack's chest for more than twenty-five years.

He was a frightened widower, set in his ways and sick with worry for both his boys, but none of that made it hurt less. Someone else did come. Janie Moore, already told that her own son was missing, visited Jack, wrote to him and fussed over him. Jack had begun keeping his promise before he knew he would have to.

Ecclesiastes says that when you make a vow, you should pay it without delay. Neither young man believed in God when they made that promise. But Jack kept his word for more than thirty years. fields.title: Mrs Moore
fields.body_html:
“Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.” — James 1:27 (KJV)

When Jack went back to Oxford in January 1919, Janie Moore and Maureen came too. As soon as the university rules allowed, he moved in with them. For the next thirty years he had no other home.

They were poor. Mrs Moore had an irregular allowance from her estranged husband; Jack had his scholarship and an allowance from his father. They moved again and again between cheap rented rooms, and Mrs Moore took in lodgers. Jack shopped, washed up, ran errands, tutored Maureen in Latin, walked the dog, and studied when he could find a quiet hour. Even so, he took three Firsts, the highest grade Oxford gives: two in classics and philosophy, and one in English, a whole degree he finished in a single year. It still didn't get him a job, and for two more years the household scraped by.

Albert was told almost nothing. He didn't know that Jack was living with Mrs Moore, or that the money he sent was partly keeping her household. Jack deceived him, sometimes by silence and sometimes with direct lies, for about ten years. Later Lewis counted this as one of the great sins of his life. When he looked back on his years of unbelief, it wasn't his wrong ideas that troubled him most. It was this.

So what was the relationship? Every biographer has asked, and none can say for certain. She was twenty-six years older than him and still legally married. He called her Minto, after a brand of sweets, and often referred to her as his mother, and many people assumed she was. Some biographers think that in the early years they were lovers. Others are sure it was always like a son and an adopted mother. No letter or record settles it, and Lewis, who was otherwise open about his sins, never explained it. The honest answer is that we don't know. If it began as an affair, it seems clear it did not stay one, and certainly not after his conversion.

What nobody disputes is what came after. For more than thirty years Jack supported her, lived with her and looked after her. It wasn't an easy house. She was generous and hardworking, but also possessive and anxious, forever calling him away from his work for errands that could have waited. Some friends resented it for him. He almost never complained. Later he wrote with unusual wisdom about the small irritations of family life, and about how love is learned at home or not at all. He learned it in that house.

In May 1925 the job finally came: Jack was elected a Fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, to teach English. Albert was overjoyed, and Jack wrote him one of the warmest letters he ever sent. It still said nothing about Mrs Moore.

James says pure religion is looking after orphans and widows in their trouble. Mrs Moore wasn't technically a widow, but in practice she and Maureen had been abandoned, and Paddy's death took away their last support. A young atheist took them in, and James would have recognised what he was doing. But this chapter shows the other side too: the same young man was lying to his own father. You can be doing something good and something wrong at the same time. God sees both, and he wants both brought into the light.

One thing to do this week: is there something you are hiding from a parent or someone who loves you? If it is safe to do so, take one honest step: tell the truth about one thing, or talk to a trusted adult about how to.

study_questions.answer: Living with a demanding person taught him patience, and later he wrote wisely about the small irritations of family life and how love is learned at home.

fields.title: The Most Reluctant Convert
fields.body_html:
“Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?” — Psalm 139:7 (KJV)

In May 1926, at a faculty meeting, Lewis met a new professor named J. R. R. Tolkien. His first impression wasn't warm. But Tolkien loved the same northern myths Lewis had loved since boyhood, and soon the two were sitting up late in Lewis's rooms talking about gods and heroes. Tolkien was a devout Catholic. He didn't argue people into faith. He simply took both Christianity and myth completely seriously, and couldn't see why they should be kept apart.

Other friends unsettled him too. Owen Barfield argued with him for years and taught him to question the idea that whatever is newer must be truer. Nevill Coghill astonished him by being the cleverest man in the room and a Christian. One after another, the most interesting people Lewis met seemed to be believers. He noticed, and it bothered him.

Lewis later described his conversion not as a search but as a hunt, with himself as the prey. His defences fell one by one. He began the 1920s believing that nothing existed but matter. But he came to see that if our thoughts are only the side effects of atoms moving, there is no reason to trust them, including the thought that only matter exists. So he retreated to believing in a vague Absolute Mind behind the universe, one that made no demands and couldn't be prayed to. That was comfortable. Then his reading kept betraying him. The writers he loved most, like the poet George Herbert, were Christians, and Chesterton's The Everlasting Man made Christian history make sense. And one evening in 1926 one of the toughest atheists he knew remarked that the historical evidence for the Gospels was surprisingly good. Lewis was shaken. If even this man couldn't keep the door shut, where could he hide?

In the summer of 1929 Albert fell ill with cancer. Jack went home and sat with him for weeks, and the long hours together softened some of the old bitterness. When the doctors saw no immediate danger, he went back to Oxford. Within days a telegram called him home. He arrived too late. Albert died on 25 September 1929. Jack was crushed by grief and guilt: ten years of deceiving his father and mocking him behind his back, and now nothing could be put right.

Then, alone in his college room one night, he stopped resisting. He knelt and prayed, admitting that God was God. He called himself “the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England.” He dated this to the summer of 1929. But the biographer Alister McGrath read his letters in order and found no sign of a change in 1929 and clear signs of one in 1930. Most scholars now think Lewis misremembered and that it happened in 1930, after his father's death, though some still defend his date. If they are right, a son who had wronged his earthly father and could no longer make amends found himself on his knees before another Father.

Be clear about what this was. He now believed in God. He did not yet believe in Christ. He started going to church and to college chapel, because he thought that if you believe in God you should show it. He didn't enjoy it, and he disliked hymns. He went anyway, obeying before he fully believed.

Psalm 139 asks where you could go to get away from God, and answers: nowhere. Lewis tried every hiding place a brilliant mind could find, and God was already there in each one. If you feel God closing in on you, and part of you would rather he didn't, that isn't a bad sign. Some of the best stories start with a reluctant yes.

One thing to do this week: read Psalm 139 slowly. Underline every place where the writer says God is already there. Then honestly finish this sentence: “The place I've been trying to hide from God is ...”

study_questions.question: How did Lewis describe his own conversion to belief in God?
study_questions.answer: Not as a search but as a hunt, with himself as the quarry. Each position he retreated to fell, until he knelt as “the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England.”

study_questions.question: Why do most scholars think Lewis came to believe in God in 1930, not 1929?
study_questions.answer: Alister McGrath read his letters in order and found no sign of change in 1929 but clear signs in 1930, so Lewis probably misremembered the year when writing decades later. Some still defend 1929.

study_questions.question: Was Lewis a Christian once he knelt and prayed?
study_questions.answer: Not yet. He believed in God but not in Christ. He began going to church out of obedience before he had full faith.

fields.title: Myth Became Fact
fields.body_html:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.” — John 1:14 (KJV)

After Albert's death, Little Lea was sold. With Jack's share of the money and some of Mrs Moore's, the household at last bought a home in 1930: the Kilns, a low brick house at the foot of Shotover Hill outside Oxford, with eight acres of woods and a pond in an old clay pit. Lewis loved it at first sight and lived there for the rest of his life.

For more than a year after kneeling down, he believed in God but not in Christ. He prayed, went to church, read the Gospels and tried to obey his conscience. What he couldn't do was make sense of the Christian story. How could the death of a man in Palestine nineteen hundred years ago have anything to do with him now? How could one man's death take away another's sins?

On Saturday 19 September 1931 he had two friends to dinner at Magdalen: Tolkien, and Hugo Dyson, a quick, witty lecturer who was also a Christian. Afterwards the three walked out along Addison's Walk, the path beside the river behind the college, and talked for hours about myth.

Lewis loved the ancient stories of a god who dies and comes back to life. When he met them in pagan writers they moved him deeply, and he didn't demand to know what they meant. But when he met the same pattern in the Gospels, he demanded explanations. Tolkien and Dyson turned this around. Why not let the story of Christ move him the way the old myths did, before he could explain it? And then they made the decisive point. The story of Christ was like those myths, with all their power and beauty, but with one immense difference: it really happened. At a real time, in a real place, under a real Roman governor. The old stories had been dim hints of the true one. The myth had become fact.

Tolkien went home at about three in the morning. Lewis and Dyson walked and talked until nearly four.

Nine days later, on 28 September 1931, Warnie drove Jack to Whipsnade Zoo on his motorcycle, with Jack in the sidecar. It was a sunny morning. There was no new argument and no dramatic moment. Lewis later put it simply:

“When we set out I did not believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and when we reached the zoo I did.”

He compared it to waking up and realising you are already awake. (Most biographers give that date for the ride; one or two place it a little earlier the same month.) On 1 October he wrote to Arthur Greeves that he now believed in Christ, and that the night talk with Dyson and Tolkien had a great deal to do with it. Warnie, meanwhile, had found his own way back to faith that same year. On Christmas Day 1931 Jack took Communion at Holy Trinity, the village church near the Kilns, for the first time since that miserable confirmation in 1914. This time he believed. He stayed a faithful member of that church for the rest of his life.

John writes that the Word became flesh and lived among us. That is what finally reached Lewis: God didn't just give the world a beautiful idea; he stepped into history. Sometimes the barrier to faith isn't a lack of evidence but the wrong way of looking. And sometimes faith arrives quietly, without fireworks. If yours feels undramatic, that's fine. Lewis's arrived in a sidecar.

One thing to do this week: read John 1:1-14. Then write one sentence about what difference it makes to you that the story of Jesus actually happened, rather than being just a good story.

study_questions.question: What was the key point Tolkien and Dyson made on Addison's Walk?
study_questions.answer: That the story of Christ had all the power of the old myths of a dying and rising god, but with one difference: it really happened in history. The myth had become fact.

study_questions.question: Where was Lewis when he came to believe that Jesus is the Son of God?
study_questions.answer: In the sidecar of Warnie's motorcycle on the way to Whipsnade Zoo, on 28 September 1931 according to most biographers.

study_questions.question: Why was Christmas Day 1931 significant?
study_questions.answer: Lewis took Communion at Holy Trinity, Headington Quarry, for the first time since his unbelieving confirmation in 1914, and this time he believed.

At the centre were Lewis, Warnie and Tolkien, with others coming and going, nearly all Christians and nearly all writers or scholars. Lewis thought real friends were people looking at the same truth together, not people who flattered each other.

When the Second World War began in 1939, Lewis was forty. Evacuee schoolgirls from London came to live at the Kilns, and the bachelor who claimed not to like children found he rather enjoyed them. He joined the Home Guard and patrolled Oxford at night with a rifle. The writer Charles Williams moved to Oxford and became a close friend. Williams believed that Christians can, in a real sense, carry part of one another's burdens in love. Lewis never forgot it. When Williams died after an operation in May 1945, Lewis found, to his own surprise, that his faith was strengthened rather than shaken.

In 1940 he published The Problem of Pain, about how a good God can allow suffering, for a country waiting to be bombed. Then, sitting in church one Sunday, he had an idea: letters from an experienced devil to a junior devil who was trying to lead a young Englishman away from God, with everything upside down. You need to understand it well enough to say it plainly, and to respect the person who is asking.

fields.title: Who Knows the Worst About You?
fields.body_html:
“Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.” — James 5:16 (KJV)

By 1941 strangers were writing to tell Lewis that he had changed their lives. That is hard for anyone to hear, and harder for someone who had spent his youth wanting to be thought clever. He knew he was proud. He feared he might become an expert on religion and stop being a Christian. So he did three things about it, and they matter as much as any of his books.

First, in October 1940 he began going to confession. He chose an elderly priest, Father Walter Adams, a gentle, humble man of over seventy. Lewis admitted that he dreaded it; what might seem a small step to others was a huge one for him. Afterwards he found it had done him good, and he went almost every week for twelve years, until Father Adams died. Confessing to a priest is unusual among Protestants, and Lewis never said everyone should do it. He chose it because he knew his own heart and didn't trust himself to deal with it alone. He needed someone who would hear the worst, not be impressed by his fame, and tell him the truth.

Second, money. As royalties poured in, he had a horror of getting rich on religion. With Owen Barfield's help he set up a charity called the Agape Fund, from the Greek word for love. Two-thirds of his royalties went into it and were given away quietly to widows, struggling clergy, students and families who couldn't pay school fees. He lived simply: shabby clothes, cheap tobacco, worn furniture.

Third, letters. Every morning he spent an hour or two answering strangers, by hand, with a pen dipped in ink: the doubting, the grieving, the lonely, children, even cranks. Warnie typed thousands of replies for him. Lewis complained about the work and kept doing it until a few weeks before he died. And when he promised to pray for someone, he did.

Then came a famous evening. In 1942 Lewis had become president of the Socratic Club, a student society where Christians and unbelievers argued in public, each side hearing the strongest case against it. On 2 February 1948 a young philosopher named Elizabeth Anscombe, herself a devout Catholic, read a paper attacking one argument in his book Miracles. She wasn't attacking Christianity, only what she thought was a bad argument for it. It was a sharp evening, and some who were there thought Lewis had been beaten. He seems to have agreed that she had made a real point. He was low afterwards and didn't hide it. Then he went back and rewrote the chapter for a later edition.

A legend grew that he was so humiliated that he gave up defending the faith and retreated into children's stories. That is mostly false. He led the Socratic Club for six more years and wrote Christian books for the rest of his life. Narnia had been in his head for years. Anscombe herself later called the legend nonsense. His pride was hurt. His faith was not.

James puts confession and prayer side by side and promises healing. Over the years, people who knew Lewis noticed that the arrogant, cutting young man had become, without losing his edge, humble and kind. That kind of change usually happens slowly, through ordinary habits nobody sees. And it helps to have at least one person who knows the worst about you and loves you anyway.

One thing to do this week: ask yourself who knows the worst about you. If no one does, think of one wise, trustworthy Christian, a parent, pastor or mentor, you could be honest with, and take one step toward that conversation.

fields.title: Burdens and a Wardrobe
fields.body_html:
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” — Galatians 6:2 (KJV)

In public, the years after the war were the peak of Lewis's fame; in 1947 an American news magazine put him on its cover. In private they were among the hardest of his life. He was worn out from the war years, and the two people he lived with were both falling apart.

Mrs Moore was in her seventies, in pain from ulcers on her legs and less and less able to move. She grew more anxious and demanding, quarrelled with the maids, and wanted Jack at her side constantly. Visitors watched him called away again and again for some small crisis. Warnie's diary is full of fury at what he saw as her tyranny. Jack hardly ever complained. He nursed her, fetched and carried for her, and listened.

Warnie, meanwhile, was drinking. After the war it became binges that lasted days or weeks and sometimes ended in hospital. In 1947, on holiday in Ireland, he was taken into a hospital at Drogheda run by Irish nuns, and Jack crossed the sea to be with him. The nuns nursed Warnie back many times. In no record that survives did Jack lecture him. He worried, prayed, brought him home and forgave him. But there were times when the brother he depended on most couldn't be depended on at all.

In June 1949 Jack collapsed with a serious infection and exhaustion. Friends told him the household was killing him. He wouldn't hear of changing it. He had made a promise.

In April 1950 Mrs Moore had to move into a nursing home. He visited her almost every day, often crossing Oxford in the middle of a heavy working day to sit with a woman who was often confused. She died in January 1951, aged seventy-eight. He admitted to friends both relief and real grief. He had kept his promise to Paddy for more than thirty years.

Oxford never made him a professor. Some colleagues thought a scholar who wrote popular religious books and spoke on the radio wasn't quite respectable. He felt the slights but didn't complain in public.

And in these cramped, exhausting years he wrote Narnia. Since he was about sixteen he had carried a picture in his head of a faun carrying an umbrella and parcels through a snowy wood. In 1948 and 1949 he finally wrote the story. Tolkien disliked it intensely; another friend loved it, and Lewis kept going. The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe appeared in 1950, with six more books after it. He insisted they weren't allegories but stories imagining what the Son of God might be like if he came into another world. Children wrote to him in thousands, and he answered them patiently, never talking down. When one child worried about loving Aslan more than Jesus, Lewis gently replied that this wasn't really possible, because the things the child loved Aslan for were the very things Jesus had done and said.

In 1954 Cambridge offered him a new professorship, and he accepted. It was the recognition Oxford had never given him.

Paul says to bear one another's burdens. Lewis carried an old woman's decline, a brother's drinking and the letters of thousands of strangers, mostly unthanked and unseen. It nearly broke his health. Yet out of those years came the books that have gone furthest of all. Carrying someone else's load is never wasted time, even when it feels as if your own life is on hold.

One thing to do this week: notice one person at home who carries a heavy load: a parent, a grandparent, a brother or sister. Quietly take one job off them without being asked, and don't mention it.

fields.title: A Bedside Wedding
fields.body_html:
“A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;” — Ecclesiastes 3:4 (KJV)

Joy Davidman was born in New York in 1915 to Jewish immigrant parents and grew up an atheist. She was astonishingly clever: university at fifteen, a master's degree at twenty, a national poetry prize in her early twenties. She joined the Communist Party, then married a fellow writer, Bill Gresham. They had two sons, David and Douglas. The marriage was unhappy. Bill drank, was unfaithful and had violent moods. One night in 1946 he phoned to say he was having a breakdown and didn't know what he would do, then hung up. Alone and helpless with two small children, Joy found, for the first time, that she was aware of God. She ended up on her knees.

She had been reading Lewis's books, and in January 1950 she wrote to him. Warnie remembered that her letters stood out: lively, direct, and plainly a match for Jack in argument. They first met for lunch in Oxford in September 1952. She was blunt, funny, fearless and not at all overawed, and he enjoyed it hugely. That Christmas, while she was staying at the Kilns, Bill wrote asking for a divorce. The next year she moved to England with her boys. She was poor, and Lewis quietly helped pay the boys' school fees.

In 1956 the government refused to let her stay in England. Lewis couldn't bear to lose her company, so he offered a solution: a civil marriage, a legal formality only, to give her the right to stay. On 23 April 1956 they were married at a register office. They didn't live together, and he didn't think of it as a real marriage.

Then, in October 1956, Joy's thigh bone snapped. Cancer had eaten it away, and it had spread. The doctors didn't expect her to live long. Facing the loss of her, Lewis realised that he loved her. The legal marriage now felt like a mockery. He wanted to be married before God, but the Bishop of Oxford refused, because Joy was divorced. Lewis wouldn't go behind his back.

In March 1957 Lewis asked a former pupil, a priest named Peter Bide, to come and pray for Joy's healing. When Bide understood the whole situation, he decided he could not in conscience refuse to marry them. On 21 March 1957, in her hospital room, with Warnie there, he married them, then laid his hands on Joy and prayed. She was sent home to the Kilns to die.

She didn't. To her doctors' astonishment, the cancer stopped and then went back, and her bones began to heal. By the end of the year she could walk with a stick. Lewis believed God had answered prayer, but he never treated it as proof of anything. Meanwhile his own bones began to weaken. Remembering Charles Williams, he wondered whether he had been allowed to carry a little of her pain. He didn't claim it. He thought it possible, and was glad if it was so.

The next three years were the happiest of his life. Joy brought the shabby old house back to life, argued with him as an equal, read his drafts and shared his faith. In 1958 they had a honeymoon in Ireland. In October 1959 the cancer returned. In April 1960, in pain, she toured Greece with him. On 13 July 1960 she died, with him beside her. She was forty-five.

Ecclesiastes says there is a time to weep and a time to dance. Lewis and Joy were given a short time to dance, overshadowed by illness the whole way through, and they took it as a gift anyway. Don't wait for perfect conditions to love people well.

One thing to do this week: tell someone you love, in words or in writing, one specific thing you are grateful for about them. Do it now, not someday.

study_questions.answer: Against all expectation, her cancer stopped and went back, her bones healed, and she lived about three more years.

fields.title: Men Must Endure
fields.body_html:
“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:” — 2 Timothy 4:7 (KJV)

After Joy died, Lewis did what he had always done with experience: he wrote it down. In some old exercise books, almost every day, he recorded what grief was doing to him. The first sentence has become one of the most quoted he ever wrote:

“No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear.”

He described the restlessness, the inability to concentrate, the awkwardness of people who didn't know what to say, and his terror that his memories of Joy were already fading. He was honest about his faith too. He didn't stop believing in God. What frightened him was that God might be cruel rather than loving. When he turned to God, he felt he met a shut door and silence. He wrote things he would never have let a student write in an essay, because they were what he felt and he had decided not to lie.

Slowly the notebooks change. He began to see that a man who is shouting can't hear, and that his picture of God, like his picture of Joy, had partly been his own invention, which the real one kept breaking. He didn't find answers, but the questions began to look different, and he came to a kind of peace. He published the notebooks under a made-up name as A Grief Observed. After his death it came out under his own name, and it has helped millions of grieving people, because it doesn't pretend.

Lewis became guardian of Joy's sons, David, sixteen, and Douglas, fourteen, and treated them with kindness and respect. When David chose to live as an observant Jew, Lewis supported him, asking Jewish scholars for advice and helping him learn Hebrew.

His own health was failing. In July 1963 he had a heart attack, fell into a coma, and was given the last rites. About an hour later he woke up and asked for a cup of tea. He said, half seriously, that nearly dying had been gentle and that he was almost sorry to be sent back, like Lazarus. He resigned from Cambridge, and he and Warnie spent quiet last weeks together at the Kilns, reading, doing crosswords and remembering their childhood. He was calm about dying.

On 22 November 1963, at about half past five, Warnie heard a crash and found him collapsed at the foot of his bed. Within minutes he was dead, a week short of his sixty-fifth birthday. About an hour later President Kennedy was shot in Dallas, and the death of an Oxford don was barely noticed. Warnie was too overcome to go to the funeral. He chose the gravestone, and on it he had cut the line from their mother's calendar of 1908: “Men must endure their going hence.”

Paul's words, “I have kept the faith,” are not about never doubting. After Joy died, Lewis went down into the dark and came back up. Faith isn't the absence of anguish. It's what holds when anguish has done its worst. If you are grieving, you can be honest with God, even angry; the psalms do it, and Jesus did it on the cross. And if grief or darkness ever feels like more than you can carry, tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live.

One thing to do this week: write a short, honest letter to God about the hardest thing you are carrying. Don't tidy it up. Keep it, and read it again in a month to see what has changed.

study_questions.question: What was A Grief Observed, and why did it help people?
study_questions.answer: Lewis's notebooks written after Joy's death, published under a made-up name. It helps grieving people because it is honest and doesn't pretend to explain suffering away.

study_questions.question: Did Lewis lose his faith after Joy died?
study_questions.answer: No. He felt God was silent and feared God might be cruel, and he wrote that down honestly, but he came through to a kind of peace and went on praying and going to church.

study_questions.question: What words are on Lewis's gravestone, and why?
study_questions.answer: “Men must endure their going hence,” the line from King Lear on his mother's calendar the day she died in 1908. Warnie chose it.
